newsitem.title: UK: Poland's Kwasniewski pushes to join EU and NATO.
newsitem.headline: Poland's Kwasniewski pushes to join EU and NATO.

text.p: Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski said on Thursday that integration with both the European Union and NATO are his principal priorities for his country.
In a speech to the Royal Institute of International Affairs during his two-day trip to Britain, Kwasniewski said joining both organisations was important for the people of Poland.
"We perceive them as historical opportunities not to be missed," he said.

"The Poles have reached the conclusion that security to them means first of all Poland's membership in the North Atlantic Alliance. Poland is the one country in Central Europe where more than 82 percent of the population supports full membership of NATO."

Kwasniewski, a former communist who replaced Solidarity leader Lech Walesa as president last year, argued that the enlargement of NATO would strengthen the stability and security of the entire European continent, including Russia.
Kwasniewski received a boost on Tuesday, when U.S. President Bill Clinton used a campaign speech to pledge that NATO would admit new members by 1999.
Describing NATO as dynamic and complex, Kwasniewski said it should have four overrriding features.
"It should be cohesive, effective, credible and it should also display a sense of co-responsibility for the security and stability of the whole of Europe," he said.
"Poland is willing and able to make a substantial contribution to the strengthening of each and all of the aforementioned features."
Kwasniewski stressed that Poland sees itself becoming one of the pillars of NATO, not just an outpost.
"We are confident that Poland's accession to NATO will lead to a projection of stability and security into areas stretching beyond our eastern frontier."

Referring to Russia, he said his country's relations with Moscow were developing in a positive and promising fashion and that the two countries have managed to overcome their "the emotional heritage of the past."
He also called for a partnership agreement between NATO and Ukraine to satisfy Ukraine's security interests.

"We are preparing for swift accession talks, which would allow Poland to take a permanent seat among NATO members by the time the alliance celebrates its 50th anniversary in three years' time," he concluded.
During his brief visit, Kwasniewski will hold talks with Prime Minister John Major and opposition leaders and visit Queen Elizabeth.

Kwasniewski's visit to London comes as the lower house of Poland's parliament voted to pass a bill liberalising the country's tough anti-abortion law -- a change strongly opposed by the Roman Catholic Church.
